lessons.title: The parabola y = ax^2 + q
objectives: You will be able to describe the effect of a and q on the graph of y = ax^2 + q
You will be able to determine the turning point, axis of symmetry, domain and range of a parabola
You will be able to sketch y = ax^2 + q

keyWords.meaning: A function whose rule contains x squared as its highest power of x.
The smooth U-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic function.
The highest or lowest point on a parabola.
The vertical line through the turning point that divides the parabola into two matching halves.
The set of all input values for which a function is defined.
The set of all output values that a function can produce.
The point where a graph cuts the y-axis.
A point where a graph cuts the x-axis.

blocks.text:
Grade 10 showed that y = ax^2 + q is a quadratic function and its graph is a parabola. The number a controls the shape and the direction (smile or frown); q moves the whole graph up or down.

In this lesson we read these two numbers from the equation and use them to find the main features of the graph.
blocks.speech: In Grade 10 you met quadratic functions. A quadratic function written as y equals a x squared plus q has a parabola as its graph. The number a controls the shape and whether the graph opens upwards or downwards. The number q moves the whole graph up or down. In this lesson we read a and q from the equation and use them to find the main features of the graph.

blocks.text:
For y = ax^2 + q, the value q is added to every output of y = ax^2. So every point of y = ax^2 moves q units up when q > 0 and q units down when q < 0.

The turning point moves from (0;0) to (0;q). The y-intercept is also (0;q), because at x = 0, y = q.
blocks.speech: For y equals a x squared plus q, the value q is added to every output of y equals a x squared. So every point of the graph moves q units up when q is greater than zero, and q units down when q is less than zero. The turning point moves from zero, zero to zero, q. The y-intercept is also at zero, q, because when x is zero, y is q.

blocks.caption: The same parabola y = x^2 moved vertically by q. The turning point and y-intercept both sit at (0;q).
blocks.speech: The picture shows three parabolas with the same shape. The middle one is y equals x squared. The upper one is moved two units up, so q equals two. The lower one is moved two units down, so q equals minus two. In each case the turning point is on the y-axis at zero, q. The y-intercept is the same point.

blocks.problem: For f(x) = x^2 - 4, determine the turning point, the axis of symmetry, the domain, the range, the y-intercept and the x-intercepts.

steps.reason: Compare the equation with y = ax^2 + q.
For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q).
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the turning point.
A quadratic function is defined for every real x.
a > 0, so the minimum y-value is q.
Substitute x = 0, or use the fact that the y-intercept is (0;q).
Let y = 0 to find the x-intercepts.

steps.line: Turning point (0;-4); axis of symmetry x = 0; domain x in R; range y ≥ -4; y-intercept (0;-4); x-intercepts (-2;0) and (2;0)
steps.reason: State all the required features.

blocks.answer: Turning point (0;-4); axis of symmetry x = 0; domain x in R; range y ≥ -4; y-intercept (0;-4); x-intercepts (-2;0) and (2;0)
blocks.speech: The function is f of x equals x squared minus four. Comparing with y equals a x squared plus q, a is one and q is minus four. The turning point is zero, minus four. The axis of symmetry is the line x equals zero. The domain is all real numbers. Since a is positive, the range is y greater than or equal to minus four. The y-intercept is zero, minus four. Set y equal to zero. Then x squared minus four equals zero, so x squared equals four, so x equals minus two or x equals two. The x-intercepts are minus two, zero and two, zero. The turning point is zero, minus four and the range is y greater than or equal to minus four.

blocks.text:
In y = ax^2 + q, a changes the width and the direction of the parabola. If a > 0 the parabola opens upwards (smile) and has a minimum turning point. If a < 0 it opens downwards (frown) and has a maximum turning point.

A larger |a| makes it narrower; a value of a closer to 0 makes it wider.
blocks.speech: In y equals a x squared plus q, a changes the width and the direction of the parabola. If a is positive, the parabola opens upwards and has a minimum turning point. If a is negative, it opens downwards and has a maximum turning point. A larger size of a makes the parabola narrower. A value of a closer to zero makes it wider.

blocks.caption: The sign of a decides smile or frown; the size of a decides how narrow the parabola is.
blocks.speech: The picture shows three parabolas. The one with a equals two is narrow and opens upwards. The one with a equals one half is wider and opens upwards. The one with a equals minus one opens downwards, so it is a frown. The sign of a decides whether the turning point is a minimum or a maximum. The size of a decides how narrow or wide the curve is.

blocks.problem: Sketch f(x) = -2x^2 + 8. Give the turning point, axis of symmetry, domain, range and intercepts.

steps.reason: Compare with y = ax^2 + q; a negative means a frown and a maximum turning point.
For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q).
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the turning point.
A quadratic function is defined for every real x.
The maximum y-value is q because a < 0.
Substitute x = 0, so y = 8.
Let y = 0 to find the x-intercepts.

steps.line: x-intercepts (-2;0) and (2;0); turning point (0;8); range y ≤ 8
steps.reason: State the main features for the sketch.

blocks.answer: x-intercepts (-2;0) and (2;0); turning point (0;8); range y ≤ 8
blocks.speech: The function is f of x equals minus two x squared plus eight. Here a is minus two, which is negative, and q is eight. The parabola is a frown with a maximum turning point at zero, eight. The axis of symmetry is x equals zero. The domain is all real numbers. The range is y less than or equal to eight. The y-intercept is zero, eight. Set y equal to zero. Then minus two x squared plus eight equals zero, so two x squared equals eight, so x squared equals four, so x equals minus two or x equals two. The x-intercepts are minus two, zero and two, zero. The turning point is zero, eight and the range is y less than or equal to eight.

blocks.text:
To sketch y = ax^2 + q: first use a to decide smile or frown and width. Then plot the turning point (0;q) and draw the axis of symmetry x = 0.

Find the y-intercept (0;q) and, if they exist, the x-intercepts by solving 0 = ax^2 + q. Finally state domain and range: domain is always x in R; range is y ≥ q if a > 0, and y ≤ q if a < 0.
blocks.speech: To sketch y equals a x squared plus q, first use a to decide whether the parabola is a smile or a frown and how wide it is. Then plot the turning point at zero, q and draw the axis of symmetry x equals zero. Find the y-intercept at zero, q and, if they exist, the x-intercepts by solving zero equals a x squared plus q. Finally state the domain and range. The domain is always all real numbers. The range is y greater than or equal to q if a is positive, and y less than or equal to q if a is negative.

blocks.caption: The parabola y = x^2 - 4. Its turning point is (0;-4), its axis of symmetry is x = 0, and its x-intercepts are (-2;0) and (2;0).
blocks.speech: The picture shows the parabola y equals x squared minus four. Its turning point is marked at zero, minus four on the y-axis. The axis of symmetry is the y-axis, the line x equals zero. The parabola cuts the x-axis at minus two, zero and at two, zero. The y-intercept is the same as the turning point, zero, minus four.

blocks.problem: Sketch g(x) = 1/2 x^2 + 3. Determine the turning point, axis of symmetry, domain, range, y-intercept and x-intercepts.

steps.reason: Compare with y = ax^2 + q; a positive means a smile and a minimum turning point.
For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q).
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the turning point.
A quadratic function is defined for every real x.
The minimum y-value is q because a > 0.
Substitute x = 0, so y = 3.
Let y = 0 to find the x-intercepts; a square cannot equal a negative number.

steps.line: No x-intercepts; turning point (0;3); range y ≥ 3
steps.reason: State the main features for the sketch.

blocks.answer: No x-intercepts; turning point (0;3); range y ≥ 3
blocks.speech: The function is g of x equals one half x squared plus three. Here a is one half, which is positive, and q is three. The parabola is a smile with a minimum turning point at zero, three. The axis of symmetry is x equals zero. The domain is all real numbers. The range is y greater than or equal to three. The y-intercept is zero, three. Set y equal to zero. Then one half x squared plus three equals zero, so one half x squared equals minus three, so x squared equals minus six. A square cannot be negative, so there are no x-intercepts. The turning point is zero, three and the range is y greater than or equal to three.

blocks.problem: A parabola has equation y = ax^2 - 3 and passes through the point (2;5). Find a, then state the range of the parabola.

steps.reason: Substitute x = 2 and y = 5 into the equation.
Simplify two squared.
Add 3 to both sides.
Divide both sides by 4.
Replace a by 2 in the given equation.

steps.line: a = 2 > 0, so the minimum value is q = -3
steps.reason: A positive a gives a minimum turning point, and q is the minimum output.
State the value of a and the range.

blocks.answer: a = 2; range y ≥ -3
blocks.speech: A parabola has equation y equals a x squared minus three and passes through the point two, five. Substitute x equals two and y equals five. Then five equals a times two squared minus three. That gives five equals four a minus three. Add three to both sides to get eight equals four a. Divide by four, so a equals two. The equation is y equals two x squared minus three. Since a is positive, the parabola has a minimum turning point. The minimum value is q, which is minus three. Therefore a equals two and the range is y greater than or equal to minus three.

question.prompt: Determine the turning point of y = -3x^2 + 5.
steps: Compare with y = ax^2 + q: q = 5.
For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q).
question.why: Some learners use the value of a or use 0 instead of q for the y-coordinate.
question.rightWay: For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is always (0;q), so here it is (0;5).

blocks.hint: Look at the number added to the x^2 term.
blocks.speech: Determine the turning point of y equals minus three x squared plus five. Compare with y equals a x squared plus q. Here q is five. For y equals a x squared plus q the turning point is zero, q. So the turning point is zero, five.

blocks.wrong: For y = 2x^2 - 3 the turning point is (0;0).
blocks.right: For y = 2x^2 - 3 the turning point is (0;-3).
blocks.why: The value q shifts the whole parabola vertically. The turning point is (0;q), not always the origin.
blocks.speech: A common mistake is to take the turning point of y equals two x squared minus three as zero, zero. That ignores the minus three. The correct turning point is zero, minus three. The value q shifts the whole parabola vertically. The turning point is zero, q, not always the origin.

blocks.text: Every parabola y = ax^2 + q has axis of symmetry x = 0 and turning point (0;q). The sign of a tells you whether q is a minimum or a maximum, and therefore decides the range. The y-intercept is always (0;q); x-intercepts are found by solving 0 = ax^2 + q.
blocks.speech: Every parabola y equals a x squared plus q has axis of symmetry x equals zero and turning point at zero, q. The sign of a tells you whether q is a minimum or a maximum, and therefore decides the range. The y-intercept is always zero, q. The x-intercepts are found by solving zero equals a x squared plus q.

summary: The graph of y = ax^2 + q is a parabola with turning point (0;q) and axis of symmetry x = 0.
q moves the parabola vertically; the y-intercept is always (0;q).
If a > 0 the parabola opens upwards and the range is y ≥ q.
If a < 0 the parabola opens downwards and the range is y ≤ q.
The domain is always x in R.
Find x-intercepts by solving 0 = ax^2 + q.

practice.prompt: Determine the y-intercept of y = 3x^2 - 2.
practice.why: Some learners use q but write the point with the coordinates swapped.
practice.rightWay: At the y-axis x = 0, so y = q = -2. The point is (0;-2).

practice.prompt: Determine the turning point of y = -x^2 + 4.
steps: Compare with y = ax^2 + q: q = 4.
For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q).
practice.why: The negative value of a is often mistaken for the y-coordinate of the turning point.
practice.rightWay: The y-coordinate of the turning point is q, which is 4, so the turning point is (0;4).

practice.prompt: If y = ax^2 + 2 passes through (1;5), find a.
practice.why: Some learners divide before subtracting q from both sides.
practice.rightWay: Substitute the point, then subtract 2 from both sides before dividing by 1 squared.

practice.prompt: Which statement gives the range of y = 2x^2 - 5?
steps: a = 2 > 0, so the minimum value is q.
practice.why: A positive a gives a minimum, but learners sometimes reverse the inequality.
practice.rightWay: Since a > 0, the parabola has a minimum y-value of q = -5, so the range is y ≥ -5.

practice.prompt: How many x-intercepts does y = x^2 + 2 have?
steps: No real solution, so there are 0 x-intercepts.
practice.why: Some learners assume every parabola cuts the x-axis twice.
practice.rightWay: Solving gives x^2 = -2, which has no real solution, so the graph has no x-intercepts.

practice.prompt: The graph of y = ax^2 + q has turning point (0;3) and passes through (2;7). Find a.
practice.why: Some learners read the turning point as (q;0) and use the wrong q.
practice.rightWay: For y = ax^2 + q the turning point is (0;q), so q = 3. Then substitute the other point to find a.

practice.prompt: Which equation has a maximum turning point at (0;-1)?
steps: A maximum turning point needs a < 0.
practice.why: A maximum needs a negative a, and q must be the y-coordinate of the turning point.
practice.rightWay: Choose the equation with a < 0 and q = -1, which is y = -x^2 - 1.

lessons.title: Shifting the parabola: y = a(x + p)^2 + q
objectives: You will be able to explain the effect of p on the graph of a parabola
You will be able to find the turning point, intercepts and axis of symmetry of y = a(x + p)^2 + q
You will be able to sketch a shifted parabola and state its domain and range

keyWords.meaning: The U-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic function.
The lowest or highest point of a parabola, where it changes direction.
The vertical line through the turning point that cuts the parabola into two mirror-image halves.
A slide of the whole graph left or right without changing its shape.
The set of all input values (x-values) for which the function is defined.
The set of all output values (y-values) that the function actually takes.
The point where the graph crosses the y-axis, found by putting x = 0.
A point where the graph crosses the x-axis, found by putting y = 0.

blocks.text:
In lesson 1 you drew parabolas of the form y = ax^2 + q. The value of a fixed the shape, and q moved the graph up or down.

Now one more constant joins them: y = a(x + p)^2 + q. The number p slides the same parabola left or right, and q still slides it up or down. Written in this form, the equation hands you the turning point, the axis of symmetry and the range.
blocks.speech: In the last lesson you drew parabolas of the form y equals a x squared plus q. The value of a fixed the shape, and the value of q slid the whole graph up or down. Today one more constant joins them, and we work with y equals a times the square of x plus p, plus q. The new number p slides the same parabola left or right, while q still slides it up or down. Written in this form, the equation hands you the turning point, the axis of symmetry and the range.

blocks.text:
The bracket (x + p) is zero when x = -p, and that is where the parabola turns. So the turning point is (-p; q) and the axis of symmetry is the line x = -p.

If p > 0 the graph moves p units to the LEFT. If p < 0 the graph moves p units to the RIGHT. The sign of p works opposite to what you may expect: (x - 3)^2 moves the graph 3 units right, and there p = -3.
blocks.speech: Look at the bracket x plus p. It is zero when x equals minus p, and that is exactly where the parabola turns. So the turning point is at minus p and q, and the axis of symmetry is the vertical line x equals minus p. When p is positive the graph moves p units to the left. When p is negative the graph moves p units to the right. The sign of p works the other way round from what many people expect: x minus 3 squared moves the parabola 3 units to the right, and that means p equals minus 3.

blocks.caption: y = x^2, y = (x - 2)^2 (2 units right) and y = (x + 1)^2 (1 unit left). All three curves have the same shape.
blocks.speech: The picture shows three parabolas on one set of axes. The plain one in the middle is y equals x squared, with its turning point at the origin. The second one has moved 2 units to the right, and its equation is y equals x minus 2 squared; its turning point is at 2 and 0. The third one has moved 1 unit to the left, and its equation is y equals x plus 1 squared; its turning point is at minus 1 and 0. All three curves have exactly the same shape.

blocks.text:
In y = a(x + p)^2 + q: a gives the shape and the direction, p gives the horizontal shift, and q gives the vertical shift and the y-coordinate of the turning point.

The range follows from the turning point. If a > 0, y ≥ q. If a < 0, y ≤ q. The domain is always x ∈ R.
blocks.speech: Here is how to read any equation of this form. The number a gives the shape and the direction: when a is positive the parabola smiles and the turning point is a minimum, and when a is negative it frowns and the turning point is a maximum. The number p gives the horizontal shift, and q gives the vertical shift. The range follows from the turning point: when a is positive, y is greater than or equal to q, and when a is negative, y is less than or equal to q. The domain is always all real numbers.

blocks.problem: For f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 2, write down the turning point, the axis of symmetry, the intercepts, the domain and the range.

steps.reason: Compare with y = a(x + p)^2 + q; x - 3 is x + (-3), so p = -3.
Substitute p = -3 and q = 2 into the formula for the turning point.
The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the turning point.
A positive a makes a smile, so the turning point is the lowest point.
Every point on the y-axis has x = 0.

steps.line: x-intercepts: 0 = (x - 3)^2 + 2, so (x - 3)^2 = -2, which has no real solution
steps.reason: A square can never be negative, so the graph does not cross the x-axis.
All x-values are allowed, and the smallest y-value is the minimum value 2.

blocks.answer: Turning point (3; 2); axis of symmetry x = 3; y-intercept (0; 11); no x-intercepts; domain x ∈ R; range y ≥ 2
blocks.speech: The function is f of x equals x minus 3 squared plus 2. Compare it with y equals a times x plus p squared plus q: a is 1, x minus 3 is x plus minus 3, so p is minus 3, and q is 2. The turning point is minus p and q, that is 3 and 2. The axis of symmetry is the line x equals 3. Since a is positive, the parabola smiles, so 3 and 2 is a minimum. For the y-intercept put x equal to zero: zero minus 3 squared is 9, plus 2 is 11, so the point is 0 and 11. For the x-intercepts put y equal to zero: x minus 3 squared equals minus 2, and no real number squared is negative, so there are no x-intercepts. The domain is all real numbers and the range is y greater than or equal to 2.

blocks.problem: For g(x) = -2(x + 1)^2 + 8, find the turning point, axis of symmetry, intercepts, domain and range. Use these to sketch the graph.

steps.reason: Compare with y = a(x + p)^2 + q; x + 1 is x + p with p = 1.

steps.line: Turning point: (-1; 8), and it is a maximum because a < 0
steps.reason: Turning point is (-p; q); a negative a makes a frown.
The vertical line through the turning point.
Put x = 0 to find where the graph cuts the y-axis.
Put y = 0 to find where the graph cuts the x-axis.
Add 2(x + 1)^2 to both sides and divide by 2.

steps.line: x + 1 = 2 or x + 1 = -2, so x = 1 or x = -3, giving (1; 0) and (-3; 0)
steps.reason: Taking a square root gives two answers, one positive and one negative.
All x-values are allowed; the largest y-value is the maximum value 8.

blocks.answer: Turning point (-1; 8); axis x = -1; y-intercept (0; 6); x-intercepts (-3; 0) and (1; 0); domain x ∈ R; range y ≤ 8
blocks.speech: The function is g of x equals minus 2 times x plus 1 squared plus 8. Here a is minus 2, p is 1 and q is 8. The turning point is minus p and q, that is minus 1 and 8, and because a is negative it is a maximum. The axis of symmetry is x equals minus 1. For the y-intercept put x equal to zero: minus 2 times 1 squared plus 8 is 6, so the point is 0 and 6. For the x-intercepts put y equal to zero: minus 2 times x plus 1 squared plus 8 equals zero, so x plus 1 squared equals 4. Then x plus 1 is 2 or x plus 1 is minus 2, so x is 1 or x is minus 3, and the points are 1 and 0 and minus 3 and 0. The domain is all real numbers and the range is y less than or equal to 8.

When you sketch, work through the same steps every time. First, look at the sign of a to decide whether the parabola smiles or frowns. Second, write down the turning point, minus p and q. Third, draw the axis of symmetry, the vertical line x equals minus p. Fourth, find the y-intercept by putting x equal to zero. Fifth, find the x-intercepts by putting y equal to zero and solving. Then state the domain, which is all real numbers, and the range, which you read off q.

blocks.problem: Sketch h(x) = -1/2 (x + 1)^2 + 2. Show the turning point, the axis of symmetry and all intercepts, and state the domain and range.

steps.reason: Compare with y = a(x + p)^2 + q.

steps.line: Turning point (-1; 2), a maximum because a < 0
steps.reason: Turning point is (-p; q); the negative a makes a frown.
Vertical line through the turning point.
Put x = 0.
Add 1/2 (x + 1)^2 to both sides and multiply by 2.

steps.line: x + 1 = 2 or x + 1 = -2, so x = 1 or x = -3, giving (1; 0) and (-3; 0)
steps.reason: A square root has a positive and a negative answer.
All x allowed; the largest y-value is the maximum value q = 2.

blocks.answer: Turning point (-1; 2); axis x = -1; y-intercept (0; 3/2); x-intercepts (-3; 0) and (1; 0); domain x ∈ R; range y ≤ 2
blocks.speech: Sketch h of x equals minus one half times x plus 1 squared plus 2. Here a is minus one half, p is 1 and q is 2. The turning point is minus 1 and 2, and since a is negative it is a maximum. The axis of symmetry is x equals minus 1. For the y-intercept put x equal to zero: minus one half times 1 squared is minus one half, plus 2 gives three halves, so the point is 0 and three halves. For the x-intercepts put y equal to zero: x plus 1 squared equals 4, so x plus 1 is 2 or minus 2, giving x equals 1 or x equals minus 3, that is the points 1 and 0 and minus 3 and 0. The domain is all real numbers and the range is y less than or equal to 2.

question.prompt: Write down the coordinates of the turning point of f(x) = (x + 2)^2 - 9.
steps: x + 2 is x + p, so p = 2, and q = -9
question.why: The sign of p is often copied across, which gives (2; -9).
question.rightWay: The bracket x + 2 is zero when x = -2, so the turning point is (-2; -9).

blocks.hint: Use the rule that the turning point is (-p; q).
blocks.speech: Write down the coordinates of the turning point of f of x equals x plus 2 squared minus 9.

blocks.why: The bracket is zero when x = -3, so the graph is y = x^2 - 1 shifted 3 units to the left. The x-coordinate of the turning point is -p, not p.
blocks.speech: A common mistake is to read the turning point of y equals x plus 3 squared minus 1 as 3 and minus 1. The correct turning point is minus 3 and minus 1. The bracket x plus 3 is zero when x is minus 3, so the graph is the parabola y equals x squared minus 1 shifted 3 units to the left. The x-coordinate of the turning point is minus p, not p.

blocks.text:
To shift a parabola that is already written down, replace x. For a shift of m units to the right, replace x with (x - m). For a shift of m units to the left, replace x with (x + m).

A shift up or down only changes the number added at the end. Shifting never changes the shape, so a stays the same.
blocks.speech: To shift a parabola that is already written down, you replace x. For a shift of m units to the right, replace x with x minus m. For a shift of m units to the left, replace x with x plus m. A shift up or down only changes the number added at the end. Shifting never changes the shape, so a stays exactly the same.

blocks.caption: y = x^2 moves 3 units right and 2 units down to give y = (x - 3)^2 - 2, with turning point (3; -2).
blocks.speech: The picture shows y equals x squared, and the same parabola after it has been moved 3 units to the right and 2 units down. The new turning point is at 3 and minus 2, and the new equation is y equals x minus 3 squared minus 2. The shape of the two curves is identical; only the position has changed.

blocks.problem: The parabola y = x^2 is shifted 3 units to the right and 2 units down. Write down the equation of the new parabola and its turning point.

steps.line: Shift 3 units right: replace x with (x - 3), giving y = (x - 3)^2
steps.reason: A shift to the right replaces x with x minus the number of units.

steps.line: Shift 2 units down: subtract 2, giving y = (x - 3)^2 - 2
steps.reason: A shift down changes the number added at the end of the expression.
Write the answer in the form y = a(x + p)^2 + q.
Substitute p = -3 and q = -2.

blocks.answer: y = (x - 3)^2 - 2, turning point (3; -2)
blocks.speech: The parabola y equals x squared is shifted 3 units to the right and 2 units down. A shift of 3 to the right means replacing x with x minus 3, which gives y equals x minus 3 squared. A shift of 2 down means subtracting 2, which gives y equals x minus 3 squared minus 2. In this form a is 1, p is minus 3 and q is minus 2, so the turning point is 3 and minus 2. The answer is y equals x minus 3 squared minus 2, with turning point 3 and minus 2.

question.why: Many learners take only the positive square root and lose the solution x = -1.
question.rightWay: After dividing by -3 you get (x - 1)^2 = 4, so x - 1 = 2 or x - 1 = -2.

blocks.hint: Divide both sides by -3 first, then take the square root of both sides.
blocks.speech: Determine the x-intercepts of f of x equals minus 3 times x minus 1 squared plus 12.

blocks.text:
Every parabola y = a(x + p)^2 + q is the basic parabola y = ax^2 moved p units sideways and q units up or down.

Read the turning point as (-p; q) and the axis of symmetry as x = -p. Then find the intercepts, and take the domain and the range from the turning point.
blocks.speech: Every parabola of this form is the basic parabola y equals a x squared moved p units sideways and q units up or down. Read the turning point as minus p and q, and the axis of symmetry as x equals minus p. Then find the intercepts, and take the domain and the range from the turning point. That is the whole method for this lesson.

summary: y = a(x + p)^2 + q is the parabola y = ax^2 shifted p units sideways and q units up or down.

lessons.title: Average gradient between two points
objectives: You will be able to calculate the average gradient between two points on a curve
You will be able to find the average gradient using f(a + h) and f(a)
You will be able to explain what happens as the two points move closer together

keyWords.meaning: The steepness of a line, calculated as the change in y divided by the change in x
The gradient of the straight line joining two points on a curve
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve there
The straight line that passes through two points on a curve
The set of all allowed input (x) values of a function
The point where a parabola changes direction, its highest or lowest point

blocks.text:
You already know how to find the gradient of a straight line: gradient = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1). A straight line has the same gradient everywhere.

A curve is different. On a parabola like y = x^2 the steepness changes from point to point. So for a curve we talk about the average gradient between two points: the gradient of the straight line that joins them.
blocks.speech: You already know how to find the gradient of a straight line. A straight line has the same steepness everywhere. A curve is different: on a parabola the steepness changes from point to point. So for a curve we talk about the average gradient between two points. It is simply the gradient of the straight line that joins those two points on the curve.

blocks.caption: The parabola y = x^2 with the straight line joining P(1; 1) and Q(3; 9)
blocks.speech: The picture shows the parabola y equals x squared. Two points sit on it: P at one comma one, and Q at three comma nine. The straight line drawn through them is the chord. Its gradient is the average gradient of the curve between P and Q. Notice the curve is steeper than the line in some places and flatter in others, so the line only gives an average.

blocks.text:
To find the average gradient between two points on a curve:
1. Use the x-values to find the y-values from the equation of the curve.
2. Apply the gradient formula: (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).

In function notation, if the points are P(a; f(a)) and Q(a + h; f(a + h)), then:
average gradient = (f(a + h) - f(a))/h.

Here h is the horizontal distance between the two points.
blocks.speech: Here is the method. First, use each x-value in the equation of the curve to find the matching y-values. Second, use the ordinary gradient formula. In function notation, if the points are P at a and f of a, and Q at a plus h and f of a plus h, then the average gradient is f of a plus h, minus f of a, all divided by h. The letter h is the horizontal gap between the two points.

blocks.problem: Find the average gradient of f(x) = x^2 between the points where x = 1 and x = 3.

steps.reason: Substitute x = 1 into the equation to get the y-value of the first point
Substitute x = 3 into the equation to get the y-value of the second point
Apply the gradient formula using the two points (1; 1) and (3; 9)
Replace f(3) with 9 and f(1) with 1, and 3 - 1 = 2
Simplify the fraction

blocks.speech: Find the average gradient of f of x equals x squared between x equals one and x equals three. Step one: f of one is one squared, which is one. Step two: f of three is three squared, which is nine. Step three: the average gradient is f of three minus f of one, divided by three minus one. That is nine minus one over two, which is eight over two, giving four. The average gradient is four.

blocks.problem: Find the average gradient of f(x) = x^2 between P(a; f(a)) and Q(a + h; f(a + h)). Simplify your answer.

steps.reason: The y-value at P is the function value at a
Expand the square using (a + h)^2 = a^2 + 2ah + h^2
Use the gradient formula
Substitute the y-values and the x-values
Cancel a^2 - a^2 in the numerator and a cancels in the denominator
Take out the common factor h so it can be cancelled
Cancel the h on top and bottom

blocks.answer: 2a + h
blocks.speech: Now a general version on the same curve. For f of x equals x squared, find the average gradient between the point with x-value a and the point with x-value a plus h. The first y-value is a squared. The second is a plus h squared, which expands to a squared plus two a h plus h squared. The gradient formula gives that numerator minus a squared, over a plus h minus a. The top becomes two a h plus h squared, the bottom is just h. Factorise h out of the top and cancel, leaving two a plus h. This is a formula we will reuse.

blocks.problem: Use the result average gradient = 2a + h for f(x) = x^2 to find the average gradient between P where x = 2 and Q where x = 5.

steps.reason: Match the given x-values to the labels a and a + h
Solve for h, the horizontal distance between the points
Use the general result from the previous example
Substitute a = 2 and h = 3
Simplify

blocks.speech: We can use the general result two a plus h instead of substituting every time. For f of x equals x squared, the average gradient between x equals two and x equals five: here a is two, and a plus h is five, so h is three. Then the average gradient is two times two plus three, which is seven. Check it the long way: f of five is twenty five, f of two is four, and twenty five minus four over three is seven. Same answer, faster.

question.prompt: Use the formula average gradient = 2a + h for f(x) = x^2 to find the average gradient between the points where x = 2 and x = 4.
question.why: Learners often use a + h as h itself, forgetting to subtract a to find h.
question.rightWay: Identify a = 2 and a + h = 4, so h = 4 - 2 = 2. Then substitute into 2a + h: 2(2) + 2 = 6.

blocks.hint: First work out h from the two x-values, then substitute a and h into 2a + h.
blocks.speech: Your turn. For f of x equals x squared, use the formula two a plus h to find the average gradient between x equals two and x equals four. Hint: first find h by subtracting the smaller x-value from the bigger one.

blocks.text:
What happens when the two points move closer together? The value of h gets smaller.

For f(x) = x^2 the average gradient is 2a + h. As h gets closer to 0, the average gradient gets closer to 2a. The line through the two points turns into a line touching the curve at one point only. That line is called the tangent, and its gradient is the gradient of the curve at that point.

This idea is the heart of calculus, which you will meet in Grade 12.
blocks.speech: Now the big idea. What happens when the two points move closer together? The value of h gets smaller. For f of x equals x squared, the average gradient is two a plus h, so as h approaches zero the average gradient approaches two a. The straight line through the two points becomes a line that touches the curve at one single point. That line is called the tangent, and its gradient is the gradient of the curve at that point. This idea is the heart of calculus, coming in Grade 12.

blocks.caption: As the second point slides towards the fixed point, the chord becomes the tangent line
blocks.speech: The picture shows the parabola y equals x squared with one fixed point marked. The straight line drawn there is the tangent: it touches the curve at that one point and matches its steepness. This is what the chord becomes when the two points move together.

blocks.problem: Given f(x) = -2x^2. Find the average gradient between A where x = 1 and B where x = 3. Hence find the gradient of the curve at A.

steps.reason: Substitute x = 1 to find the y-value of A
Substitute x = 3 to find the y-value of B
Use the gradient formula between the points (1; -2) and (3; -18)
Substitute the values; subtracting -2 means adding 2 in the numerator
Simplify the fraction
The gradient at a point is the average gradient with h = 0; the general result for f(x) = -2x^2 is -4a - 2h

blocks.answer: Average gradient -8; gradient at A is -4
blocks.speech: Here is a curve that opens downwards. Given f of x equals minus two x squared, first find the average gradient between x equals one and x equals three. f of one is minus two. f of three is minus eighteen. The average gradient is minus eighteen minus minus two, over two, which is minus sixteen over two, so minus eight. Now for the gradient at the point where x equals one, we let h equal zero. The general result for this curve is minus four a minus two h, so at a equals one the gradient is minus four.

question.prompt: Given g(x) = -x^2 + 1, find the average gradient of the curve between the points where x = -2 and x = 1.
question.why: Learners often forget the minus sign in front of the bracket and get g(-2) = 5 instead of -3.
question.rightWay: Substitute carefully: -(-2)^2 means -(+4), so g(-2) = -3. Then use the gradient formula: (0 - (-3))/(1 - (-2)) = 3/3 = 1.

blocks.hint: Substitute each x-value carefully: -(-2)^2 means first square -2, then make the answer negative.
blocks.speech: Your turn. Given g of x equals minus x squared plus one, find the average gradient between x equals minus two and x equals one. Hint: the minus sign applies after you square, so be careful with the signs.

blocks.wrong: Average gradient = (f(3) - f(1))/(1 - 3) for the points x = 1 and x = 3
blocks.why: The x-values must go in the same order top and bottom: y2 - y1 over x2 - x1. If you flip the bottom only, the sign of the gradient changes and the answer is wrong.
blocks.speech: Here is a common mistake. When finding the average gradient between x equals one and x equals three, some learners write f of three minus f of one, but then divide by one minus three. That flips the denominator but not the numerator, so the sign of the gradient comes out wrong. The right way is to keep the order the same: f of three minus f of one, divided by three minus one. Both coordinates go from the first point to the second point.

blocks.wrong: f(a + h) - f(a) = (a + h)^2 - a^2 = h^2, so the gradient is h^2/h = h
blocks.right: f(a + h) - f(a) = (a + h)^2 - a^2 = 2ah + h^2, so the gradient is 2a + h
blocks.why: You must expand (a + h)^2 as a^2 + 2ah + h^2 before subtracting a^2. The a^2 terms cancel, but the middle term 2ah stays and cannot be dropped.
blocks.speech: Another common mistake: learners subtract a squared from a plus h squared and write just h squared. That skips the expansion. The right way is to expand a plus h squared as a squared plus two a h plus h squared. Then a squared minus a squared cancels, but the middle term two a h remains, along with h squared. After dividing by h the correct average gradient is two a plus h, not h. Always expand the square fully before you cancel.

blocks.text:
To sum up the whole method:
1. Average gradient between two points = gradient of the chord joining them = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).
2. In function notation: (f(a + h) - f(a))/h.
3. For f(x) = x^2 this simplifies to 2a + h.
4. As h approaches 0 the chord becomes the tangent and the average gradient becomes the gradient at the point.

In the exam, show the substitution and every line of simplification; marks are given for the working.
blocks.speech: Let us pull it together. The average gradient between two points on a curve is the gradient of the straight line joining them: y two minus y one over x two minus x one. In function notation that is f of a plus h minus f of a, over h. For the curve f of x equals x squared it simplifies neatly to two a plus h. And as the points move together, h approaches zero and the chord becomes the tangent. In the exam, show all your working; marks are given for each line.

In function notation: average gradient = (f(a + h) - f(a))/h
For f(x) = x^2 the average gradient simplifies to 2a + h
As h gets closer to 0, the chord becomes the tangent and the average gradient becomes the gradient at that point
Keep the x-values in the same order in the numerator and the denominator

lessons.title: The hyperbola y = a/(x + p) + q
objectives: You will be able to identify the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of a hyperbola
You will be able to describe the effects of a, p and q on the hyperbola
You will be able to sketch a hyperbola with its axes of symmetry, domain and range

keyWords.meaning: The graph of an equation of the form y = a/(x + p) + q, made of two curved branches in opposite regions.
One of the two separate curved pieces that together make up a hyperbola.
A straight line that a graph runs towards but never touches.
The line x = -p, which the branches of the hyperbola approach but never cross.
The line y = q, which the branches of the hyperbola approach for large inputs and outputs.
The set of all input values x for which the function is defined.
The set of all output values y that the function can produce.
A line that folds the graph onto itself, so each branch lands on the other branch.

blocks.text:
A hyperbola is the graph of y = a/x, where a is a non-zero constant. The two curved pieces are called branches. The branches never touch the x-axis or the y-axis, because x is never 0 and a/x is never 0.

We write shifted hyperbolas as y = a/(x + p) + q. The numbers p and q slide the branches, and a controls which opposite regions they lie in. This lesson shows how to read all three numbers straight from the equation.
blocks.speech: A hyperbola is the graph of y equals a over x, where a is a non-zero constant. The two curved pieces are called branches. The branches never touch the x-axis or the y-axis, because x is never zero, and a over x is never zero. We write shifted hyperbolas as y equals a over x plus p, plus q. The numbers p and q slide the branches, and a controls which opposite regions they lie in. This lesson shows how to read all three numbers straight from the equation.

blocks.text:
The line that a branch runs towards but never touches is an asymptote. For y = a/(x + p) + q:

- x + p = 0 makes the denominator zero, so the function is undefined there. The vertical asymptote is x = -p.
- As x becomes very large, a/(x + p) shrinks towards 0, so y approaches q. The horizontal asymptote is y = q.

Both are always written as lines: x = -p and y = q.
blocks.speech: The line that a branch runs towards but never touches is an asymptote. In the equation y equals a over x plus p, plus q: x plus p equals zero makes the denominator zero, so the function is undefined there, and the vertical asymptote is x equals minus p. As x becomes very large, a over x plus p shrinks towards zero, so y approaches q, and the horizontal asymptote is y equals q. Both are always written as lines: x equals minus p and y equals q.

blocks.caption: The standard hyperbola y = 1/x. The vertical asymptote is x = 0 (the y-axis) and the horizontal asymptote is y = 0 (the x-axis). One branch lies in the first quadrant, the other in the third.
blocks.speech: The picture shows the standard hyperbola y equals one over x. It has two branches. One branch lies in the first quadrant and the other in the third quadrant. The branches come close to the y-axis and to the x-axis but never touch them. The y-axis is the vertical asymptote x equals zero, and the x-axis is the horizontal asymptote y equals zero.

blocks.text:
The sign of a decides which two opposite regions the branches occupy, measured from the crossing point (-p; q).

If a > 0, the branches lie in the first and third regions, going down to the left and up to the right of the crossing point. If a < 0, the branches lie in the second and fourth regions.

A larger |a| pushes the branches further from the crossing point; a smaller |a| pulls them closer. The value of a never moves the asymptotes.
blocks.speech: The sign of a decides which two opposite regions the branches occupy, measured from the crossing point minus p and q. If a is greater than zero, the branches lie in the first and third regions, going down to the left and up to the right of the crossing point. If a is less than zero, the branches lie in the second and fourth regions. A larger size of a pushes the branches further from the crossing point, and a smaller size of a pulls them closer. The value of a never moves the asymptotes.

blocks.caption: Two hyperbolas on the same axes. y = 1/x has a > 0: branches in the first and third regions. y = -1/x has a < 0: branches in the second and fourth regions.
blocks.speech: The picture shows two hyperbolas on the same axes. The graph of y equals one over x has a positive and its branches sit in the first and third regions. The graph of y equals minus one over x has a negative and its branches sit in the second and fourth regions. Both graphs have the same asymptotes, the x-axis and the y-axis. Only the sign of a has changed, and only the regions of the branches have changed.

blocks.text:
q shifts the whole graph up or down. In y = a/(x + p) + q every point moves up by q units, down if q < 0, and the horizontal asymptote moves with it to y = q.

p works the other way round. The equation contains x + p, so the vertical asymptote is at x = -p. For p > 0 the line x = -p is negative, so the graph shifts left by p units; for p < 0 it shifts right. Read p, then change its sign.
blocks.speech: q shifts the whole graph up or down. In y equals a over x plus p, plus q, every point moves up by q units, or down if q is negative, and the horizontal asymptote moves with it to y equals q. p works the other way round. The equation contains x plus p, so the vertical asymptote is at x equals minus p. For p greater than zero the line x equals minus p is negative, so the graph shifts left by p units. For p less than zero it shifts right. Read p, then change its sign.

blocks.caption: The hyperbola y = 2/(x + 1) + 3 compared with y = 1/x. Here p = 1 so the graph shifts 1 unit left, q = 3 so it shifts 3 units up, and a = 2 pushes the branches further out.
blocks.speech: The picture shows the hyperbola y equals two over x plus one, plus three, compared with the standard hyperbola y equals one over x. Here p is one, so the graph shifts one unit to the left, and q is three, so it moves three units up. The asymptotes are now the vertical line x equals minus one and the horizontal line y equals three. The value of a is two, so the branches are further from the crossing point than the branches of the standard hyperbola.

the branches approach this line but never cross it
for large x the fraction 3/(x - 2) shrinks to 0, so y approaches 1

First, x minus two equals zero gives x equal to two, because the denominator is zero at x equal to two, so the function is undefined there. The vertical asymptote is x equal to two. The range is y a real number, y not equal to one, because three over x minus two is never zero, so the output never equals one. The final answer is domain x not equal to two, and range y not equal to one.

blocks.text:
Why is the output never equal to q? Rearrange: y - q = a/(x + p). If y - q were 0, then a/(x + p) would be 0, which is impossible because a is not 0. So y ≠ q for every input.

In exactly the same way x + p = 0 is impossible, so x ≠ -p. That single fact gives the domain x ≠ -p, the range y ≠ q, and the two asymptotes, all at once.
blocks.speech: Why is the output never equal to q? Rearrange the equation: y minus q equals a over x plus p. If y minus q were zero, then a over x plus p would be zero, which is impossible because a is not zero. So y is never equal to q. In exactly the same way, x plus p equals zero is impossible, so x is never equal to minus p. That single fact gives the domain, the range and the two asymptotes, all at once.

blocks.speech: The problem: find the x-intercept and the y-intercept of g of x equals minus two over x plus one, plus four. First the y-intercept. Let x equal zero, because every point on the y-axis has x equal to zero. Then y equals minus two over zero plus one, plus four, which is minus two plus four, which is two. So the y-intercept is the point zero and two. Now the x-intercept. Let y equal zero, because every point on the x-axis has y equal to zero. So zero equals minus two over x plus one, plus four. First, x minus one is x plus minus one, so p is minus one and a is minus two and q is one. The asymptotes are x equal to one and y equal to one. Because a is negative, the branches lie in the second and fourth regions around the point one and one. The y-intercept: let x equal zero, and y equals minus two over minus one, plus one, which is three, so the point zero and three. The x-intercept: let y equal zero, then zero equals minus two over x minus one, plus one, so minus one equals minus two over x minus one, then x minus one equals two, so x equals three, and the point is three and zero. The axes of symmetry pass through one and one. Using y equals x plus c gives c equal to zero, so y equals x. Using y equals minus x plus c gives c equal to two, so y equals minus x plus two. The domain is x not equal to one, and the range is y not equal to one. The final answer: asymptotes x equal to one and y equal to one, intercepts zero and three and three and zero, axes of symmetry y equals x and y equals minus x plus two, domain x not equal to one, range y not equal to one.

Find its equation. The vertical asymptote x equal to minus one gives minus p equal to minus one, so p equals one. The horizontal asymptote y equal to three gives q equals three. lessons.title: The exponential graph y = ab^(x + p) + q
objectives: You will be able to describe the effects of a, b, p and q on an exponential graph
You will be able to find the horizontal asymptote and range of an exponential function
You will be able to sketch an exponential graph

keyWords.meaning: A function of the form y = ab^(x + p) + q, where b is positive and not equal to 1.
The number b that is raised to the power x in b^x.
The horizontal line y = q that the graph gets closer to but does not cross.
The set of all possible input values x.
The set of all possible output values y.
The point where the graph crosses the y-axis, found by putting x = 0.
The point where the graph crosses the x-axis, found by putting y = 0.
A function whose graph goes up as x increases from left to right.

blocks.text:
An exponential function has the general form y = ab^(x + p) + q, where b > 0 and b is not 1. The graph is a smooth curve that has a horizontal asymptote and never crosses it.

You already know the basic curve y = b^x. Every exponential graph in this lesson is a shifted, stretched or reflected copy of that basic curve.
blocks.speech: An exponential function has the general form y equals a times b to the power x plus p, plus q, where b is greater than zero and b is not equal to one. The graph is a smooth curve with a horizontal asymptote that it never crosses. You already know the basic curve y equals b to the power x. Every exponential graph in this lesson is a shifted, stretched or reflected copy of that basic curve.

blocks.text:
For y = b^x with b > 1, the graph rises from left to right. For 0 < b < 1, the graph falls from left to right.

The basic graph y = b^x has asymptote y = 0, y-intercept (0;1), domain x ∈ R and range y > 0.
blocks.speech: For y equals b to the power x with b greater than one, the graph rises from left to right. For b between zero and one, the graph falls from left to right. The basic graph y equals b to the power x has asymptote y equals zero, y-intercept zero semicolon one, domain all real numbers and range y greater than zero.

blocks.caption: The graphs of y = 2^x and y = (1/2)^x. Both pass through (0;1) and approach the x-axis.
blocks.speech: The picture shows two graphs on one set of axes. One is y equals two to the power x, rising from left to right. The other is y equals one half to the power x, falling from left to right. Both pass through the point zero semicolon one and get closer to the x-axis.

blocks.text:
In y = ab^(x + p) + q, each parameter has a job.

q moves the graph up or down and gives the asymptote y = q. p moves the graph left or right. a stretches the graph and reflects it when a is negative. b decides growth or decay.
blocks.speech: In y equals a times b to the power x plus p, plus q, each parameter has a job. q moves the graph up or down and gives the asymptote y equals q. p moves the graph left or right. a stretches the graph and reflects it when a is negative. b decides growth or decay.

blocks.caption: q = 2 shifts y = 2^x up by 2 units. The new asymptote is y = 2.
blocks.speech: The picture shows y equals two to the power x and y equals two to the power x plus two. The second graph is the first graph moved up by two units. A dashed horizontal line shows the new asymptote y equals two. The point zero semicolon one moves to zero semicolon three.

blocks.problem: For f(x) = 2^x + 3, write down the horizontal asymptote, the range and the y-intercept.

steps.reason: Compare with y = ab^(x + p) + q.
The horizontal asymptote is y = q.

steps.line: a > 0, so the graph lies above y = 3
steps.reason: A positive a puts the graph above the asymptote.
All output values are above the asymptote.
The y-intercept is found where x = 0.
Substitute x = 0 and simplify.
The y-intercept is a point.

blocks.answer: asymptote y = 3, range y > 3, y-intercept (0; 4)
blocks.speech: The problem asks for the horizontal asymptote, the range and the y-intercept of f of x equals two to the power x plus three. Compare with the general form: a equals one, b equals two, p equals zero and q equals three. The horizontal asymptote is y equals three. Because a is positive, the graph lies above the asymptote, so the range is y greater than three. For the y-intercept, put x equals zero. Then f of zero equals two to the power zero plus three, which is one plus three, equal to four. The y-intercept is zero semicolon four.

blocks.text:
The value p shifts the graph horizontally. The expression b^(x + p) reaches the same value as b^x when x is smaller by p.

For p > 0 the graph shifts p units to the left. For p < 0 the graph shifts p units to the right.
blocks.speech: The value p shifts the graph horizontally. The expression b to the power x plus p reaches the same value as b to the power x when x is smaller by p. For p greater than zero the graph shifts p units to the left. For p less than zero the graph shifts p units to the right.

blocks.caption: p = 1 shifts y = 2^x left by 1 unit. The point (0;1) moves to (-1;1).
blocks.speech: The picture shows y equals two to the power x and y equals two to the power x plus one. The second graph is the first graph moved one unit to the left. The point zero semicolon one moves to minus one semicolon one.

steps.reason: Compare with y = ab^(x + p) + q.
The horizontal asymptote is y = q.

steps.line: a < 0, so the graph lies below y = 4
steps.reason: A negative a reflects the graph across the asymptote.
All output values are below the asymptote.
The y-intercept is found where x = 0.
Substitute x = 0.
Simplify the power and the product.
The y-intercept is a point.

Compare with the general form: a equals minus three, b equals two, p equals minus one and q equals four. The horizontal asymptote is y equals four. Because a is negative, the graph lies below the asymptote, so the range is y less than four. For the y-intercept, put x equals zero. Then y equals minus three times two to the power zero minus one, plus four. That is minus three times one half plus four, which is five halves. The y-intercept is zero semicolon five halves.

steps.reason: Compare with y = ab^(x + p) + q.
The horizontal asymptote is y = q.

steps.reason: Positive a and base greater than 1 give growth above the asymptote.
Substitute x = 0 and simplify.
The x-intercept is found where y = 0.
Write both sides with base 2 and equate the exponents.
Solve for x.
State the intercepts and the range.

blocks.answer: asymptote y = -2, intercepts (0; -3/2) and (2; 0), range y > -2
blocks.speech: The problem asks to sketch f of x equals two to the power x minus one, minus two, and give the asymptote, the intercepts and the range. Compare with the general form: a equals one, b equals two, p equals minus one and q equals minus two. The horizontal asymptote is y equals minus two. Because a is positive and b is greater than one, the graph is increasing and lies above y equals minus two. For the y-intercept, put x equals zero. Then y equals two to the power zero minus one, minus two, which is one half minus two, equal to minus three halves. For the x-intercept, put y equals zero. Then zero equals two to the power x minus one, minus two. So two to the power x minus one equals two, which is two to the power one. Therefore x minus one equals one and x equals two. The intercepts are zero semicolon minus three halves and two semicolon zero, and the range is y greater than minus two.

question.why: Some learners substitute x = 1 or forget to subtract 5.
question.rightWay: Put x = 0: 3 × 2^1 - 5 = 1, so the y-intercept is (0;1).

blocks.speech: The question is: for h of x equals three times two to the power x plus one, minus five, find the y-intercept. The hint is: the y-intercept is where x equals zero.

blocks.wrong: For y = -2 × 3^(x + 1) + 4 the range is y > 4.
blocks.right: For y = -2 × 3^(x + 1) + 4 the range is y < 4.
blocks.why: A negative a reflects the graph below the horizontal asymptote y = 4, so all outputs are less than 4.
blocks.speech: The wrong statement says that for y equals minus two times three to the power x plus one, plus four, the range is y greater than four. The right statement says the range is y less than four. A negative a reflects the graph below the horizontal asymptote y equals four, so all outputs are less than four.

blocks.text:
The domain of every exponential function y = ab^(x + p) + q is x ∈ R, because you can put any real number into the exponent.

The range depends on a. If a > 0, the graph lies above y = q, so the range is y > q. If a < 0, the graph lies below y = q, so the range is y < q.
blocks.speech: The domain of every exponential function y equals a times b to the power x plus p, plus q is all real numbers, because you can put any real number into the exponent. The range depends on a. If a is positive, the graph lies above y equals q, so the range is y greater than q. If a is negative, the graph lies below y equals q, so the range is y less than q.

blocks.caption: The graph with a < 0 is the reflection of the graph with a > 0 across the asymptote y = 3.
blocks.speech: The picture shows two curves with the same asymptote y equals three. One curve, y equals two to the power x plus three, lies above the asymptote. The other curve, y equals minus two to the power x plus three, lies below the asymptote. It is the reflection of the first curve across the line y equals three.

blocks.text:
The base b decides growth or decay when a is positive. If b > 1, the graph increases from left to right. If 0 < b < 1, the graph decreases from left to right.

A negative a reflects the graph across the asymptote, so it also reverses increasing and decreasing.
blocks.speech: The base b decides growth or decay when a is positive. If b is greater than one, the graph increases from left to right. If b is between zero and one, the graph decreases from left to right. A negative a reflects the graph across the asymptote, so it also reverses increasing and decreasing.

blocks.text:
To sketch y = ab^(x + p) + q, work in this order: draw the asymptote y = q; decide the shape from a and b; find the y-intercept with x = 0; find the x-intercept with y = 0; then draw the smooth curve approaching the asymptote.

Label the asymptote and intercepts. State the domain and the range.
blocks.speech: To sketch y equals a times b to the power x plus p, plus q, work in this order. Draw the asymptote y equals q. Decide the shape from a and b. Find the y-intercept by putting x equals zero. Find the x-intercept by putting y equals zero. Then draw the smooth curve approaching the asymptote. Label the asymptote and intercepts, and state the domain and the range.

blocks.text:
Every exponential graph y = ab^(x + p) + q is controlled by four numbers. q gives the asymptote and the range; p gives the horizontal shift; a gives reflection and stretch; b gives growth or decay.

Read q first, then a and b, then p. After that the intercepts and the sketch follow quickly.
blocks.speech: Every exponential graph y equals a times b to the power x plus p, plus q is controlled by four numbers. q gives the asymptote and the range. p gives the horizontal shift. a gives reflection and stretch. b gives growth or decay. Read q first, then a and b, then p. After that the intercepts and the sketch follow quickly.

summary: The exponential graph y = ab^(x + p) + q has horizontal asymptote y = q and domain x ∈ R.
If a > 0 the range is y > q; if a < 0 the range is y < q.
p > 0 shifts the graph left by p units; p < 0 shifts it right by p units.
The value a stretches or reflects the graph; b > 1 gives growth and 0 < b < 1 gives decay when a > 0.
Find the y-intercept with x = 0 and the x-intercept with y = 0.
Sketch by drawing the asymptote, intercepts and the correct shape.

lessons.title: The sine and cosine graphs
objectives: You will be able to sketch y = a sin x + q and y = a cos x + q
You will be able to determine the amplitude, period, intercepts and turning points
You will be able to state the domain and range of a trigonometric graph

keyWords.meaning: The maximum height of the wave above and below the middle line; it is always positive and equals |a|.
The width of one complete wave of the graph; for y = sin x and y = cos x it is 360°.
A point where the graph reaches a maximum (top) or a minimum (bottom) value.
The point where the graph crosses the x-axis, found by letting y = 0.
The point where the graph crosses the y-axis, found by letting x = 0°.
The set of all x-values the graph is drawn for, for example 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
The set of all y-values the graph reaches, for example [-2;2].
Flipping the graph; a negative value of a reflects the wave about the x-axis.

blocks.text:
In Grade 10 you met sin, cos and tan in right-angled triangles. Now we treat sin and cos as functions: the input is an angle x in degrees and the output is a number. Because each input gives exactly one output, we can draw a graph.

The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x are smooth waves. They repeat forever, so in exams we usually draw them for one or two periods, for example 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° or -180° ≤ x ≤ 180°.
blocks.speech: In Grade 10 you used sin and cos in triangles. Now we treat them as functions: the input is an angle in degrees, the output is a number, so we can draw a graph. The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x are smooth waves that repeat forever. In exams we usually draw them for one or two periods, for example from nought degrees to three hundred and sixty degrees.

blocks.caption: The basic sine wave from 0° to 360°: it starts at 0, peaks at 90°, dips to -1 at 270°.
blocks.speech: This picture shows the basic sine wave from nought to three hundred and sixty degrees. It starts at the origin, rises to a maximum of one at ninety degrees, comes back to zero at one hundred and eighty degrees, drops to a minimum of minus one at two hundred and seventy degrees, and returns to zero at three hundred and sixty degrees. One complete wave is three hundred and sixty degrees wide, so the period is three hundred and sixty degrees.

blocks.text:
The cosine wave has the same shape as the sine wave, just shifted: cos x = sin(x + 90°).

For y = cos x from 0° to 360°: it starts high at (0°;1), crosses the x-axis at 90°, reaches its minimum (180°;-1), crosses again at 270°, and returns to (360°;1). The period is 360° and the amplitude is 1, exactly like sine.
blocks.speech: The cosine wave has the same shape as the sine wave, just shifted ninety degrees. For y = cos x, the graph starts high at the point nought degrees, one, crosses the x-axis at ninety degrees, reaches its minimum of minus one at one hundred and eighty degrees, crosses again at two hundred and seventy degrees, and returns to one at three hundred and sixty degrees. The period and amplitude are the same as for sine.

blocks.caption: The basic cosine wave from 0° to 360°: it starts at 1, dips to -1 at 180°.
blocks.speech: This picture shows the basic cosine wave from nought to three hundred and sixty degrees. It starts at the point nought degrees, one, falls to zero at ninety degrees, reaches the minimum of minus one at one hundred and eighty degrees, rises back through zero at two hundred and seventy degrees, and ends at one at three hundred and sixty degrees.

blocks.text:
For y = a sin x + q and y = a cos x + q, two numbers change the basic wave.

The value of a stretches the wave vertically: the amplitude is |a|. If a is bigger than 1 the wave is taller; if 0 < a < 1 it is flatter. If a is negative, the wave is reflected about the x-axis, so peaks become dips.

The value of q shifts the whole wave up (q > 0) or down (q < 0). The range becomes [q - |a|; q + |a|].
blocks.speech: For y = a sin x + q and y = a cos x plus q, the value of a stretches the wave vertically. The amplitude is the absolute value of a. If a is bigger than one the wave is taller; if a is between nought and one it is flatter. If a is negative, the wave is reflected about the x-axis, so peaks become dips. The value of q shifts the whole wave up if q is positive, or down if q is negative. The range runs from q minus the amplitude to q plus the amplitude.

blocks.caption: Compare: y = 2 sin x is taller (amplitude 2); y = sin x + 1 is the whole wave lifted 1 up.
blocks.speech: Here are three sine waves on the same axes. The basic y = sin x has amplitude one. y = two sin x is stretched so its peaks reach two and its dips reach minus two. y = sin x plus one is the basic wave lifted one unit up, so it runs between nought and two. Notice that the period stays three hundred and sixty degrees in all three cases.

blocks.problem: Sketch y = 2 sin x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° and determine the amplitude, range, intercepts and turning points.

steps.reason: Read the values straight off the equation.
The amplitude is the absolute value of a.
There is no k in front of x, so the basic period is unchanged.
sin x = 1 at 90°, times a = 2 gives 2.
sin x = -1 at 270°, times a = 2 gives -2.
The wave runs from q - amplitude to q + amplitude.

blocks.answer: Amplitude 2, period 360°, range [-2;2], max (90°;2), min (270°;-2)
blocks.speech: Sketch y = two sin x from nought to three hundred and sixty degrees. a is two and q is nought. The amplitude is two. The period stays three hundred and sixty degrees. The maximum turning point is at ninety degrees with y value two, because sin x is one there. The minimum is at two hundred and seventy degrees with y value minus two. The x-intercepts are at nought, one hundred and eighty and three hundred and sixty degrees. The range is from minus two to two.

blocks.problem: Sketch y = cos x + 1 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° and determine the amplitude, range, intercepts and turning points.

steps.reason: Read the values straight off the equation.
The amplitude is |a| = 1; q does not change the amplitude.
q shifts the whole wave 1 unit up.
cos 0° = cos 360° = 1, then add 1.
cos 180° = -1, then add 1 gives 0.
The only point where the graph touches the x-axis is the minimum.

blocks.answer: Amplitude 1, range [0;2], max (0°;2) and (360°;2), min (180°;0)

lessons.title: Changing the period: y = sin kx and y = cos kx
objectives: You will be able to calculate the period of y = sin kx and y = cos kx using 360/k
You will be able to sketch trigonometric graphs with different periods on the same axes
You will be able to work with negative angles

keyWords.meaning: The number of degrees in one complete wave of a graph.
The maximum height of a wave above or below its middle line.
The number that multiplies x inside sin kx or cos kx.
An angle measured in the opposite direction from the usual positive direction.
A mirror image of a graph across a line.
The point where a graph cuts the x-axis.
A point where a graph has a maximum or minimum value.
The distance of a number from zero, so it is never negative.

blocks.text:
A trigonometric graph repeats. The length of one complete wave is called the period. For y = sin x and y = cos x, one complete wave takes 360°, and the amplitude is 1.

When k is placed inside the function, as in y = sin kx or y = cos kx, the wave repeats faster or slower. The value of k changes the period, not the amplitude.
blocks.speech: A trigonometric graph repeats. The length of one complete wave is called the period. For y equals sine x and y equals cosine x, one complete wave takes three hundred sixty degrees, and the amplitude is one. When k is placed inside the function, as in y equals sine of k x or y equals cosine of k x, the wave repeats faster or slower. The value of k changes the period, not the amplitude.

blocks.text:
For y = sin kx and y = cos kx, the period is 360/|k|. Use the absolute value because a period is a length and cannot be negative.

If k > 1, the wave is squeezed smaller, so the period is less than 360°. If 0 < k < 1, the wave is stretched, so the period is more than 360°.
blocks.speech: For y equals sine of k x and y equals cosine of k x, the period is three hundred sixty divided by the absolute value of k. Use the absolute value because a period is a length and cannot be negative. If k is greater than one, the wave is squeezed smaller, so the period is less than three hundred sixty degrees. If k is between zero and one, the wave is stretched, so the period is more than three hundred sixty degrees.

The period is three hundred sixty divided by the absolute value of one half. Dividing by one half is the same as multiplying by two. Three hundred sixty times two is seven hundred twenty. So the period is seven hundred twenty degrees, and the amplitude stays one.

It completes three full waves in three hundred sixty degrees, so each wave is one hundred twenty degrees. The amplitude is still one.

blocks.text:
Negative angles follow two important rules: sin(-x) = -sin x and cos(-x) = cos x. For the period, use the absolute value of k.

A negative k does not make the period negative. For sine, the graph is reflected, but the length of one wave is unchanged. For cosine, cos(-x) = cos x, so the negative sign has no effect on the graph.
blocks.speech: Negative angles follow two important rules. Sine of negative x equals negative sine x. Cosine of negative x equals cosine x. For the period, use the absolute value of k. A negative k does not make the period negative. For sine, the graph is reflected, but the length of one wave is unchanged. For cosine, cosine of negative x equals cosine x, so the negative sign has no effect on the graph.

The period is three hundred sixty divided by two, which is one hundred eighty. A negative sign does not make the period negative. So the period is one hundred eighty degrees.

Multiply both sides by the absolute value of k.
Divide 360 by 90.

Multiply both sides by the absolute value of k to get three hundred sixty equals ninety times the absolute value of k. Divide three hundred sixty by ninety to get four. Since k is positive, k equals four. So k is four.

Multiply both sides by the absolute value of k.

Put three hundred sixty divided by the absolute value of k equal to two hundred forty. Multiply both sides by the absolute value of k to get three hundred sixty equals two hundred forty times the absolute value of k. Divide three hundred sixty by two hundred forty to get three over two. Since k is positive, k equals three over two. So k is three over two.

lessons.title: The tangent graph y = a tan kx + q
objectives: You will be able to sketch y = tan x and identify its asymptotes and period
You will be able to describe the effects of a, k and q on the tangent graph
You will be able to sketch y = a tan kx + q with its asymptotes

keyWords.meaning: A function of the form y = a tan kx + q, whose graph has separate branches between vertical asymptotes and repeats every 180°/|k|.
A line that the graph approaches but never touches; for the tangent graph these are vertical lines where the function is undefined.
The smallest positive interval of x after which the graph repeats exactly.
One continuous piece of a tangent graph between two neighbouring asymptotes.
The set of all input values x for which the function is defined.
The set of all output values y that the function can produce.

blocks.text:
A tangent graph comes from the ratio tan θ = sin θ/cos θ. Where cos θ = 0 the ratio is undefined, so the graph has a vertical asymptote there. Between two asymptotes the graph has one branch, which rises from very negative to very positive values.

The standard graph y = tan θ repeats every 180°, not every 360° like the sine and cosine graphs, because the tangent ratio repeats after half a turn.
blocks.speech: A tangent graph comes from the ratio tangent theta equals sine theta divided by cosine theta. Where the cosine is zero the ratio is undefined, so the graph has a vertical asymptote there. Between two asymptotes the graph has one branch, which rises from very negative values to very positive values. The standard graph of y equals tangent theta repeats every one hundred and eighty degrees, not every three hundred and sixty degrees like sine and cosine, because the tangent ratio repeats after half a turn.

blocks.caption: The graph of y = tan x for -180° ≤ x ≤ 180°. The vertical lines at x = -90° and x = 90° are asymptotes, and the middle branch crosses the origin.
blocks.speech: The picture shows the graph of y equals tangent x from minus one hundred and eighty degrees to one hundred and eighty degrees. Two vertical lines, one at minus ninety degrees and one at ninety degrees, are the asymptotes. Between the asymptotes the curve rises steadily from far below the x-axis to far above it, crossing the origin. The middle branch runs between minus ninety and ninety degrees, and two more branches appear at the edges of the picture.

blocks.text:
For y = tan θ: the period is 180°; the asymptotes are the lines θ = 90° + k·180° for whole numbers k; the x-intercepts are at θ = k·180°, so (0°;0) is also the y-intercept; the range is y ∈ ℝ; the domain is all real θ except the asymptote values.

The graph has no maximum or minimum value, so tangent has no amplitude. Where a > 0 each branch increases from left to right.
blocks.speech: For y equals tangent theta the period is one hundred and eighty degrees. The asymptotes are the lines theta equals ninety degrees plus whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees. The x-intercepts are at whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees, so the origin is also the y-intercept. The range is all real numbers, and the domain is all real theta except the asymptote values. The graph has no maximum or minimum, so tangent has no amplitude. Where a is positive, every branch increases from left to right.

tan θ is undefined where cos θ = 0, which happens at ±90° in this interval.
Set tan θ = 0, which gives θ = k·180°.
Substitute θ = 0: tan 0° = 0.

blocks.answer: Period = 180°; asymptotes θ = -90° and θ = 90°; intercepts (-180°;0), (0°;0) and (180°;0)
blocks.speech: The problem asks for the sketch of f of theta equals tangent theta from minus one hundred and eighty to one hundred and eighty degrees, with its period, asymptotes and intercepts. First, the period is one hundred and eighty degrees, because the tangent ratio repeats after half a turn. Second, the asymptotes are theta equals minus ninety degrees and theta equals ninety degrees, because tangent is undefined where cosine is zero. Third, the x-intercepts are at minus one hundred and eighty, zero and one hundred and eighty degrees, because tangent is zero at whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees. Fourth, the y-intercept is the origin, since tangent of zero is zero. So the period is one hundred and eighty degrees, the asymptotes are theta equals minus ninety and theta equals ninety degrees, and the intercepts are minus one hundred and eighty zero, the origin, and one hundred and eighty zero.

blocks.text:
In y = a tan θ + q the value of a controls the steepness and the direction of the branches. If |a| > 1 the branches are steeper; if 0 < |a| < 1 they are flatter. If a < 0 the graph is reflected about the x-axis, so the branches fall instead of rise.

The value q shifts the whole graph q units up, or down when q < 0. The vertical asymptotes stay where they are, but the x-intercepts move, because the whole graph has risen or fallen.
blocks.speech: In y equals a tangent theta plus q, the value of a controls the steepness and the direction of the branches. If the size of a is bigger than one, the branches are steeper. If the size of a is between zero and one, they are flatter. If a is negative, the graph is reflected about the x-axis, so the branches fall instead of rise. The value q shifts the whole graph q units up, or down when q is negative. The vertical asymptotes stay exactly where they are, but the x-intercepts move, because the whole graph has risen or fallen.

The standard tangent curve; the curve y equals two tangent x minus two, which is twice as steep and sits two units lower; and the curve y equals minus tangent x, which is the standard curve reflected about the x-axis, so its branches fall instead of rise. All three graphs share the same vertical asymptotes at minus ninety and ninety degrees.

The value of a is two and q is minus two, so the branches are twice as steep and the whole graph sits two units lower. blocks.text:
In y = a tan kθ + q the value of k changes the period: Period = 180°/|k|. A larger k squeezes more branches into the same interval, so the period gets shorter. If 0 < k < 1 the branches are stretched out and the period gets longer.

The asymptotes are where kθ = 90° + n·180°, so θ = (90° + n·180°)/k. If k < 0 the graph is reflected about the y-axis, and the period uses |k|.

A larger k squeezes more branches into the same interval, so the period gets shorter. If k is between zero and one, the branches are stretched out and the period gets longer. The asymptotes are where k theta equals ninety degrees plus whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees, so theta equals ninety degrees plus whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees, all divided by k. If k is negative, the graph is reflected about the y-axis, and the period still uses the size of k.

blocks.speech: Here is the method for sketching y equals a tangent k theta plus q. First find the period, one hundred and eighty degrees divided by the size of k. Second, solve k theta equals ninety degrees plus whole multiples of one hundred and eighty degrees to get the asymptotes inside the given interval. Third, solve a tangent k theta plus q equals zero to get the x-intercepts. Fourth, put theta equal to zero to get the y-intercept. Fifth, plot one or two extra points on each branch and join them smoothly between the asymptotes.

blocks.answer: a = 2 and k = 3
blocks.speech: The graph of y equals a tangent k x has period sixty degrees and passes through the point with x equal to fifteen degrees and y equal to two. We must find a and k, with k positive. The period of a tangent graph is one hundred and eighty degrees divided by the size of k, so one hundred and eighty divided by k equals sixty, which gives k equals three. Now substitute the point: two equals a times the tangent of three times fifteen degrees, which is the tangent of forty five degrees. The tangent of forty five degrees is one, so a equals two. Therefore a equals two and k equals three.

blocks.why: Sine and cosine repeat every 360°, but tangent repeats every 180°. Using 360° gives a period that is twice too long, so the sketch will show half the correct number of branches.
blocks.speech: The wrong way uses the sine and cosine period and takes the period of tangent two theta as three hundred and sixty degrees divided by two, which gives one hundred and eighty degrees. The right way uses the tangent period, one hundred and eighty degrees divided by two, which gives ninety degrees. Tangent repeats every one hundred and eighty degrees, not every three hundred and sixty degrees, so using three hundred and sixty makes the period twice too long and the sketch shows half the number of branches.

blocks.text: Every tangent graph y = a tan kθ + q is the standard curve with three changes: a stretches or reflects the branches, k sets the period 180°/|k| and the spacing of the asymptotes, and q lifts the whole graph without moving the asymptotes. Always find the asymptotes first, then the intercepts, then plot one or two points on each branch.
blocks.speech: Every tangent graph of the form y equals a tangent k theta plus q is the standard curve with three changes. The value a stretches the branches or reflects them about the x-axis. The value k sets the period, one hundred and eighty degrees divided by the size of k, and the spacing of the asymptotes. The value q lifts the whole graph up or down without moving the asymptotes. Always find the asymptotes first, then the intercepts, then plot one or two points on each branch.

summary: The tangent graph has period 180°, asymptotes where cos θ = 0, x-intercepts at whole multiples of 180°, no amplitude, and range y ∈ ℝ.
For y = a tan kθ + q: |a| controls steepness, a < 0 reflects about the x-axis, q shifts the graph up or down, and k sets the period at 180°/|k|.
The vertical asymptotes are at θ = (90° + n·180°)/k and they do not move when q changes.
The domain excludes the asymptote values; the range is always all real numbers.
Sketch in this order: period, asymptotes, intercepts, then one or two points per branch.

practice.prompt: Write down the equation of the asymptote of y = tan 2θ inside the interval 0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°.
practice.why: Learners divide only the 90° and forget that the whole angle 2θ must equal 90° plus multiples of 180°.
practice.rightWay: Solve 2θ = 90° + n·180°, then divide by 2 to get θ = 45° + n·90°.
